newsitem.title: FRANCE: Pollution worries cloud outlook for diesel cars.
newsitem.headline: Pollution worries cloud outlook for diesel cars.

text.p: Controversy over the health effects of diesel fuel has clouded the outlook for diesel car sales in France and the French companies which make them.

Last month the proportion of new car sales powered by diesel engines fell to 36 percent in France from 50 percent a year earlier when it was more than double the market share for diesel in the rest of Europe.
The drop coincided with rising concerns about pollution in Paris and a shift in the government's attitude toward diesel, which had long benefitted from favourable tax treatment.

Health experts say the trouble with diesel engines is that they spew far more particulates into the air than engines fuelled by petrol. Particulates are micro-particles which lodge deep in people's lungs and are suspected of causing cancer.

"Of all the pollutants emitted by cars, both petrol and diesel, particulates pose the biggest health risk," said Denis Zmirou, a doctor who contributed to a pollution study issued last year by the French environmental agency ADEME.
He said diesel engines emit 30 times more particulates than other engines, and tighter European emissions standards going into effect in October will not lower those levels sufficiently.

The diesel lobby, led by Europe's biggest producer of diesel car engines PSA Peugeot Citroen, counters that diesel engines produce less carbon dioxide, which is associated with the erosion of the planet's protective ozone layer.

In recent years the French government took the view that diesel was an efficient and environmentally friendly fuel and favoured it with a lower tax rate. The gap between diesel and unleaded gasoline is around seven percentage points and was 8.5 points in 1992, the best year for the French car industry.

The favourable tax treatment benefitted French carmakers. More than half of the PSA group's Citroen and Peugeot vehicles have diesel engines, and the group sold nearly 10 percent of the 884,300 diesel engines it built last year to other companies.
Nearly half of the cars built by Renault SA have diesel engines.
"The tax policy was a form of hidden protection for the French market," said an analyst with a German brokerage house.

The drop in the market share of diesel powered cars in France contributed heavily to a 10 percent drop in the French carmakers' share of their home market over the past year, said CCFA chairman Henry Streit.

The new conservative government, however, has gradually begun to narrow the difference between the excise tax on diesel and petrol. Earlier this month, it introduced a flat six-centime per-litre tax increase on all fuel in the 1997 budget, representing a slightly larger tax proportionately for diesel.

With regulations and tax trends working against them, diesel engine manufacturers are counting on technological advances, such as direct injection, to reverse the trend or at least stabilise the trend. But analysts say the outlook is unclear.
"There is a particular threat to profitable diesel sales in France," analyst John Lawson at Salomon Brothers wrote in a recent report on European car companies.

"Peugeot is Europe's diesel leader, and in France all its medium and large cars are predominantly -- over two-thirds -- diesel-fuelled...Every contraction in share costs Peugeot extra marketing money to move relatively less competitive gasoline models," the report said.

"Like Peugeot, Renault sells a high proportion of its medium and large cars with diesel engines in France -- a high 50 percent in the first half of 1995 versus 41 percent in the first half of 1996. We expect increases in the relative petrol/diesel fuel price, and further erosion of the French domestics' share or margins on this count," it said.
